newsitem.title: CANADA: Robert Bourassa, former premier of Quebec, is dead.
newsitem.headline: Robert Bourassa, former premier of Quebec, is dead.

text.p: Former Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa died early on Wednesday in Notre-Dame hospital in Montreal after a long battle with cancer, a hospital official told Reuters. He was 63.
"It is with regret that I announce that Robert Bourassa died at 5:45 a.m. EDT (0945 GMT)," Notre-Dame spokeswoman Anne-Marie Tardif said.

Bourassa had been admitted to Notre-Dame on Aug. 17 to undergo treatment for melanoma, or skin cancer, that had spread to other parts of his body. Hospital officials said Bourassa had suffered a relapse in his three-year battle against cancer.
Flags flew at half-mast in Quebec City, the capital of this province of 7.3 million people, as tributes from Bourassa's friends, political allies and foes poured in.
"If Quebec is still part of Canada today, it is because of Robert Bourassa," Claude Charon, a former Cabinet minister with the separatist Parti Quebecois told the Canadian Broadcasting Corp.

"It was a shock to learn this morning that he had passed away. He has been a great servant of the state and was very dedicated to political life," Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said in Ottawa.
"Quebec has just lost a great man," Pierre Bibeau, Bourassa's chief of staff in the 1980s, said.

During his two terms as premier, from 1970 to 1976 and from 1985 to 1994, Bourassa was an ardent defender of Canadian unity and strove to keep Quebec in Canada. But he was also a pragmatic Quebec nationalist who took controversial measures to protect and promote the French language, spoken by the vast majority of Quebec residents.

Bourassa also took steps to promote the province's economic growth and the emergence of a French-speaking business class. He spurred the development of Quebec's hydroelectric resources in remote northern parts of the province and was instrumental in promoting North American free trade.

The lanky, bespectacled politician was premier during pivotal periods of Quebec's recent political history. Shortly after taking office for the first time, in 1970, he was confronted with the "October Crisis," when the left-wing, nationalist Front de Liberation du Quebec kidnapped the British trade commissioner and a Quebec Cabinet minister.
The trade commissioner, James Cross, was released, but the body of the Cabinet minister, Pierre Laporte, was found in the trunk of a car near Montreal.

Bourassa was re-elected in 1973, but his Liberal Party government was driven from office in 1976 by the separatist Parti Quebecois under charismatic one-time journalist and former Quebec Liberal Cabinet minister Rene Levesque.
Reviled as "the most hated man in Quebec," Bourassa went into self-imposed exile in Brussels, Paris and Boston, where he studied and taught economics.
But he staged a remarkable comeback in 1983, regaining the leadership of the Quebec Liberals. He regained the premiership two years later.

Bourassa resigned as premier in January 1994 because of cancer. His unexpected retirement may have helped clear the way for the Parti Quebecois to win power in the provincial election later that year.
Quebeckers narrowly rejected sovereignty in a provincial referendum last October.
Bourassa underwent experimental cancer treatment at the National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, in 1993 after the discovery of a chest tumour.
After resigning as premier in 1994, he taught at the University of Montreal. Tests at Montreal's Notre-Dame Hospital in June 1996 revealed that his cancer had returned.
Bourassa is survived by his wife, Andree Simard; his two children, Francois, a jazz pianist, and Michele, a psychologist; and two grandchildren.
